19739-modern-american-prose-selections:
Modern American Prose Selections, dated 1909, gathers American writing for study and reading. One piece marks the hundredth anniversary of a great American's birth. The speaker calls him one of the two greatest Americans. He ranks him among the two or three greatest men of the nineteenth century. That centenary was Abraham Lincoln's, widely celebrated in 1909.

School anthologies shaped what counted as American prose. Editors chose speeches, essays, and addresses that modeled clear writing. Lincoln pieces anchored many such collections. Students learned style by reading masters aloud. The book preserves that classroom canon in one binding. It shows which voices teachers trusted in 1909. For literary history, the table of choices matters as much as the texts.
19798-the-farringdons:
Ellen Thorneycroft Fowler set The Farringdons in England's Black Country. One street in the novel faces two worlds at once. West-side houses have sunny gardens and orchards sloping to meadows. Eastward stand tall chimneys, weird and terrible yet fascinating. Beyond the fields rise the Clee Hills and the Wrekin. Blue Welsh mountains close the far distance.

Fowler's novels mixed industry, faith, and family ambition. The Farringdons are a clan shaped by that divided landscape. Money from furnaces meets conscience from chapel and garden. Her Black Country detail comes from living beside it. The book preserves a region literature often skipped. It does so with affection and a sharp eye.
19977-the-blue-pavilions:
The Blue Pavilions is a historical romance by Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch, writing as Q. It opens at Harwich on 11 October 1673, at noonday. More than a hundred tall ships have newly returned from the Dutch War. The little seaport beside the Stour presents a lively appearance. Quiller-Couch builds the scene with a painter's patience. War's end fills the harbor with noise and color.

Q wrote sea-soaked Cornish and naval tales under that single letter. The Dutch wars gave him a rich, neglected century. Pavilions are campaign tents; blue ones suggest the fleet's shore world. His prose is consciously beautiful, sentence by sentence. This novel shows his romantic history at full sail. It is a connoisseur's adventure story.
20083-a-boswell-of-baghdad-with-diversio:
A Boswell of Baghdad, With Diversions, takes its name from James Boswell, the famed life writer. The narrator faces a work in four huge volumes that could fell a bookseller. That joke sets a tone of wit, books, and talk. Baghdad gives the book its far-off, storied frame.

Diversions, in the old sense, are side trips and bright asides. The book mixes tale, essay, and chat about books and men. Its charm lies in voice more than in plot alone. Readers who like learned humor will find a rich, rambling companion here.
20137-a-comparative-view-of-religions:
Francis T. Washburn wrote A Comparative View of Religions, a study of the world's faiths. He sets out each faith and weighs it against the Christian one. True religion, he argues, was prepared in Israel and fulfilled in Christ. In Christ, man knows his oneness with God, he writes.

Washburn grants that Islam holds truth and good in its teachings. Yet he holds that such truth was borrowed from older faiths. The book shows how one Christian writer of his era ranked all faiths. Readers get a clear, dated map of comparative religion from that standpoint.
20459-hours-in-a-library-volume-1-new-ed:
Hours in a Library gathers literary essays by Leslie Stephen, the critic and editor who shaped Victorian letters. This is the first volume, in a new edition with additions. Stephen writes about authors as a fellow worker among books, not as a distant judge.

The volume opens with a famous daydream about an old library. It seems, he writes, as if the souls of all the writers who left their work to the Bodleian were resting there. He feels he inhales learning while walking its shelves. The essays that follow keep that mix of deep reading and plain talk.
20468-the-delta-of-the-triple-elevens: The Delta of the Triple Elevens preserves service records of a World War outfit. It lists men one by one, with dates and postings. One clerk went on detached service on May 18, 1918, at Camp Meade. He rejoined Battery D on June 27 and sailed with it to France. Such lines trace how a unit was built and sent overseas.
20487-shakspere-personal-recollections:
Shakspere: Personal Recollections is a whimsical satire that claims an impossible narrator. The writer says it is well known among his close friends that he is no ordinary man. He claims to have lived forever, and to be ready to recall Shakespeare in person.

He says he sprang from the race of Strulbugs, who live forever on the island of Immortality. That island lies on the coast of Japan, and he began there more than a million years ago. The tall tale riffs on Swift's deathless Struldbrugs, and uses the joke to mock solemn Shakespeare worship.
20614-the-wonder-island-boys-the-mysteri:
The Mysteries of the Caverns, published in 1914, carries Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys deeper into their island's secrets. The boys and their professor friend keep building a working life from wreckage and raw materials. Each chapter reads like a lesson disguised as an adventure.

The contents move from recovering the lifeboat to deciding to row it around the point. The boys study alloys and their uses, and make stocks for their guns. They begin the hull of a new boat, learning what shape a hull should take. Their tame charge, Red Angel, even attempts to whistle.
20838-the-infra-medians:
A hot sales prospect waits, but the narrator of The Infra-Medians runs to his buddy Vic instead. Vic is Hope's brother, and the two have been pals since childhood. Sewell Peaslee Wright drops that bond into a tale of hidden beings.

Wright wrote brisk science fiction for the pulp magazines of his day. Infra-medians, creatures between worlds, give this tale its strange hook. Fast talk, sudden peril, and weird science drive the plot. Readers of early pulp tales will find Wright's pace and invention on show, with friendship, not just wonder, at the tale's core.
20980-a-survey-of-russian-literature-wit:
Vladimir, Grand Prince of Kiev, took Christianity for his whole nation in 988, this survey recounts. Baptised wholesale from Byzantium, Russia gained its Prince-Saint in that act. His grandmother Olga had paved the way with churches in Kiev before him.

Isabel Hapgood surveys Russian writing from chronicles to the great novelists of her day. Her 1902 book adds chosen pieces in her own English versions. Hapgood knew Russia deeply and turned its classics with rare care. Readers get both a map of a vast literature and a taste of its goods, in one trusted guide.
21044-the-willoughby-captains:
School parliament reports tangle speakers, teller, and heckling boys in The Willoughby Captains, Reed owns. The printed book simplifies what his tale tries to render by rule. That frank note fronts a reissue of Talbot Baines Reed's school classic.

Captains of house and games rule Willoughby's boy world in this tale. Honour, rivalry, and a disputed place drive its famed plot along. Reed helped invent the modern school story with books like this one. Willoughby's boys still feel alive: vain, brave, funny, and bound by codes they would die sooner than break in public.
21243-the-madigans:
Miriam Michelson's 1904 story collection follows the Madigan girls of San Francisco through ten linked tales. The first, Cecilia the Pharisee, opens with Sissy feeling virtuous before she has done anything at all. Other stories include A Pagan and a Puritan, The Shut-Ups, and The Ancestry of Irene.

Irene and her many supposed fathers appear in Orson Lowell's illustrations, including the frontispiece. The sisters scheme, pretend, write letters, and manage their widowed household with more wit than money. Michelson had written In the Bishop's Carriage, and she gives the Madigans the same quick talk and warm disorder. Kate: A Pretense and Old Mother Gibson close the set.
21244-by-canoe-and-dog-train-among-the-c:
Egerton Ryerson Young was a Hamilton pastor, newly married, when a letter from the Mission Rooms in Toronto reached his study in 1868. The Missionary Committee asked him to go as a missionary to the Indigenous peoples at Norway House in the Northwest. His memoir tells how he answered that summons.

Young travelled by canoe, dog train, and prairie trail toward Hudson Bay country, among the Cree and Saulteaux peoples named in his title. Chapters record frontier settlers, Sioux wars, and narrow escapes on the way. The book became a well-known record of Canadian Methodist mission life in the early Northwest, told by the man who lived it.
21315-the-king-s-sons:
King Ethelwulf of Wessex had four sons, and each in turn became king. George Manville Fenn's short tale follows the brothers, above all the youngest, Alfred, later Alfred the Great. Their tutor is Father Swythe, a monk, and only Alfred cares for what he teaches. The others prefer rougher pursuits.

Fenn pauses the story for a fine lesson in how illuminated manuscripts were made: the inks, the colours, the pens and brushes. Father Swythe later becomes Bishop Swithun of Winchester, whose feast day still carries a forty-days-of-rain legend. This quiet volume trades Fenn's usual cliffhangers for early English history told simply for young readers.
21316-the-adventures-of-don-lavington-no:
Lindon Lavington, called Don, works as a clerk in his uncle Josiah's Bristol sugar and tobacco office and hates the work. When office money goes missing, the real thief is plain to see, yet Uncle Josiah keeps accusing Don. George Manville Fenn then takes the boy's life apart in one night.

Don and Jem, a fellow worker who has also quarrelled at home, go out feeling ill-used and are seized by a press gang. They escape their ship in New Zealand, live among Maori friends, and help English settlers fight off an attack stirred by escaped convicts. In the end one villain proves to be the office thief all along.
21330-robert-burns:
Principal Shairp, professor of poetry at Oxford, wrote this life of Robert Burns. It was first published in 1879 and many times reprinted; this edition is from 1906. Eight chapters run from Burns's youth in Ayrshire through his two Edinburgh winters, his Border and Highland tours, and his farm at Ellisland. The move to Dumfries and the last years follow.

A closing chapter weighs Burns's character, poems, and songs together. Shairp notes that six biographies of Burns had already appeared before Carlyle's famous essay of 1828, and the count only grew. His own life stays compact and readable, aimed at students meeting Scotland's national poet in one volume.
21368-the-silver-canyon-a-tale-of-the-we:
Bart is a young hero out on the western plains with his uncle. In the middle of the nineteenth century, in George Manville Fenn's tale, he is seeking a new life. Antelope steaks cook over a dying fire as dangers gather: armed Native warriors skilled at creeping up unseen, rattlesnakes, and bears. The party finds a great rocky hill with a rich lode of silver in it.

The hill was mined long before, perhaps thousands of years earlier, and its summit gives grazing and a strong defensive post. They work the remaining ore commercially while attacks continue almost to the end. A railway at last reaches the mine, and a town of thousands follows the silver.
21443-vesty-of-the-basins:
Sarah P. McLean Greene sets her 1892 novel Vesty of the Basins in a small fishing village on the coast. A low, storm-beaten schoolhouse, a stranded schooner, and a fog horn mark the place. The horn was the gift of Melchias Tibbitts, a dead captain of the Basin.

Vesty's tale moves through meetings, courtship, a wedding, and village feasts. Captain Leezur's sly wooing and tall tales give the book much of its fun. Greene writes the local speech with a loving, exact ear. Her earlier Cape Cod Folks had made her name for just this kind of coastal portrait.
21459-dick-onslow-among-the-redskins:
Dick Onslow joins a party of emigrants bound for California in W. H. G. Kingston's Dick Onslow. The tale ranges in and near the Rocky Mountains, on the hard road west. Dick's friend, meanwhile, tells of cutting his way through Mexico and the settled States.

Rattlesnakes, bears, rockslides, and snow slides crowd the trail. Raids by hostile tribes bring shots, wounds, and nights spent hiding in bush and tree. Dick is shot through the leg and starves in sight of plenty. The book is not long, but Kingston packs each chapter with peril drawn from backwoods life.
21466-in-the-rocky-mountains:
Ralph and Clarice, brother and sister, lose both parents on the road west in W. H. G. Kingston's In the Rocky Mountains. Their farming family had left the middle states for a new life. Orphaned, the two young folk have no adult to lead them on.

A wagon train then comes by, and its chief proves to be their own uncle Jeff Crockett. Uncle Jeff never could abide folk crowding round his hut, and always moved on. He takes the children in and becomes dear to them. Clashes with Indigenous peoples, wolves, and bears fill the rest of this short, warm tale.
21739-hunting-the-lions:
Tom Brown, a hero with the plainest name in England, leads this Ballantyne hunting tale. Ballantyne spends his first chapter joking about the Browns of the world: grocers, butchers, milkmen, and doctors beyond counting. Then he takes his own Brown far from those safe streets.

The trail leads to lion country, where hunting tests nerve in a way no shop counter can. Ballantyne builds the tale on travel, camp life, and the charge of a lion at close range. His humor about the hero's name keeps the tone light between dangers. It is a sporting yarn of his classic kind, written for boys who dreamed of Africa from an English fireside.
21763-the-brentons:
Young Scott Brenton is led into the ministry by his widowed mother's secret prayers in this 1912 novel by Anna Chapin Ray. The prayer was never made to him, the narrator insists, but offered in silence and sincerity. Scott's path into the church gives the family of the title its center. Around him, the Brentons face the pulls of duty, love, and pride.

Ray was a practiced novelist of family life, with many titles to her name by 1912. Her touch here is quiet and close, following talk across tables and the small turns that change lives. The frontispiece shows young Catia in talk over a cup. It is a gentle book about faith tested inside a household.
21771-georgina-s-reasons:
Raymond Benyon loves a girl he cannot understand in this Henry James tale of 1885, and he knows it from the start. Georgina is tall and fair, with gorgeous auburn hair and a cold, beautiful eye. Her charm is real, yet Benyon feels a twinge of warning even in his happiness. Her parents are rude to him, and her singularity takes forms he cannot name.

James follows the love affair through its happy surface and its hidden cracks. Georgina has her reasons, and the tale's work is to bring them slowly into view. Benyon looks back in later years and calls his early unease a foreboding. It is a cool, exact study of a woman who will not be read like other people.
21903-the-californians:
Old California families collide with new American wealth in Gertrude Atherton's novel The Californians, published in 1898. Helena Belmont, sixteen and spoiled, tips her schoolbooks to the floor and demands the sun. Her dark-eyed friend Magdaléna Yorba has only her intelligence to set against Helena's beauty and money. Miss Phelps, their teacher, leaves the quarrel to Miss Yorba, as the opening scene jokes.

Atherton, a Californian herself, writes the passing of the Spanish dons' world with an insider's eye. Helena already knows the power of wealth, and sparkles with the insolence of it. Love, pride, and race run through the tale of the two girls. It is early Atherton: sharp, scenic, and set on showing California to readers who knew only its gold-rush face.
21931-sea-urchins:
Dockside boys and old sailors fill Sea Urchins, W. W. Jacobs's book of tales from 1899. The first story, Smoked Skipper, opens with a porter trotting a bran-new sea-chest toward Wapping Old Stairs. Its owner, a small ill-looking lad of fourteen, swears there is little about the sea he does not know. He orders his hellum turned with a captain's airs while the porter plays along for a cheap half-crown.

Other tales bring a grey parrot, a lost ship, pickled herring, and brother Hutchins. Jacobs writes the London river as a comedy stage where everyone is slightly at sea. The dialect is thick and the timing perfect. Sea Urchins catches his world young: urchins, skippers, and the men who carry their chests and their illusions.
21996-riviera-towns:
Hill towns above the French Riviera are walked one by one in Herbert Adams Gibbons's Riviera Towns, with Lester George Hornby's illustrations, copyrighted in 1920. From his study window at Théoule, Gibbons could almost count the windows of distant houses. Grasse on its hill was a constant temptation, and the two islands offshore kept watch. His chapters visit Cagnes, Saint-Paul, Vence, and Menton before the famous coast towns.

Monte Carlo, Villefranche, Nice, Antibes, and Cannes each get a chapter, with Mougins, Fréjus, and Saint-Raphaël to close. Gibbons looks past the casinos to old streets, courts where stables stood downstairs, and meadows thick with violets. The book was dedicated to Helen and Margaret, who indulged author and artist both. It is travel writing with a resident's patience.
22083-myths-and-legends-of-the-great-pla:
Katharine Berry Judson gathered Myths and Legends of the Great Plains in 1913. Judson made a career of collecting Native tales for general readers. The Plains peoples here include the Kiowa, Pawnee, Osage, and their neighbours. Their stories explain the buffalo, the stars, the seasons, and the spirit world.

One plate shows a dreamer priest's vision of the land of the dead. He crosses a prairie crowded with buffalo and ponies to find his dead brothers. Creation tales, trickster stories, and war stories stand side by side. Judson aimed to keep these tales in print for readers who would never hear a tribal storyteller. The book reflects both the tales and her era.
22220-policing-the-plains:
R. G. MacBeth wrote Policing the Plains as the real-life record of the Royal North-West Mounted Police. MacBeth, author of The Romance of Western Canada, tells the Mounties' story from their founding march west in 1874. The frontispiece shows mounted police rounding up horse thieves. The force's work was exactly that: patrol, pursue, and keep order across an immense frontier.

MacBeth follows famous marches, whisky traders, Sitting Bull's arrival, and the North-West Rebellion. He writes as an admirer, and the book is a celebration. Published in the 1920s, it fixed the Mountie legend for a generation. Here was the red coat who always got his man. He ruled the plains with a handful of riders.
22362-appreciations-and-criticisms-of-th:
Appreciations and Criticisms of the Works of Charles Dickens gathers judgments on England's great novelist. After Dickens fell ill and died, a school of criticism arose. It held, oddly, that a man wrote better when he was ill.

George Gissing, an able writer, nearly argued that Little Dorrit is Dickens's best book. That claim shows the strange turns Dickens criticism took. The volume sorts praise and blame across his career. Readers can watch taste change as distance from Dickens grew. It suits anyone who wants the arguments around the novels, not only the novels themselves, preserved in period voices.
22767-pagan-passions:
Pagan Passions is a science fiction novel of 1959. In it, the gods and goddesses of Olympus return to a modern world. Their return greatly inconveniences a man named Forrester. The catalog record names no author. Its own billing gives the recipe plainly: gods, intrigue, mystery, and danger, with the supernatural made to make sense.

For science fiction it is, the blurb insists, with the supernatural made logical, and fun too, despite the sword that hangs by a thread above Forrester's head. Divine politics, played as suspense comedy, drives the plot: old gods with old grudges, armed with very modern leverage. The book belongs to the bright, cheeky school of late-1950s science fiction, when the field delighted in dressing myth in a business suit.
22892-the-best-made-plans:
Everett B. Cole opens The Best Made Plans with a camera's eye sweeping a future city. It centers on a large sports stadium where players dash across the turf, then swings away over city scenes. The view then crosses the palace walls and drops to the Royal Guards' parade ground.

That cool, surveying gaze suits a story about schemes inside a polished state. Plans here are made by rulers and plotters alike, and the title warns how the best of them go. Cole wrote workmanlike science fiction for the magazines, strong on setting and mechanism. Readers get a future court, a watching lens, and intrigue that unfolds at a steady clip.
23066-the-prairie-traveler-a-hand-book-f:
Randolph B. Marcy offers hard-won knowledge in The Prairie Traveler, his handbook for overland expeditions. The information is so varied, and drawn from so many sources, he writes, that every new expedition still adds to his practical knowledge. A sound prairie manual, Marcy is convinced, belongs in every young traveler's kit, worth more than its weight many times over.

Marcy, an army officer, wrote the West's most trusted guidebook for the wagon and saddle era. Routes between the Mississippi and the Pacific, water, grass, camps, and encounters fill its chapters. Emigrants carried it like a spare wheel. Modern readers find in it the whole logistics of westward travel, exact, unromantic, and quietly lifesaving.
23169-the-diamond-lens:
Fitz-James O'Brien buys a microscope in The Diamond Lens. The promised instrument arrives at last, a simple Field's microscope costing perhaps fifteen dollars. For teaching purposes, the narrator judges, no better apparatus could have been chosen. A small treatise on microscopy, its history and discoveries, came with it.

From that schoolboy instrument O'Brien builds his famous tale of obsession. A diamond lens, a world within a water drop, and a beauty beyond reach complete it. Written in 1858, it stands near the head of American science fiction. The fifteen-dollar microscope does real work in the telling, grounding the wonder in a boy's budget. Every later story of microscopic worlds descends from this drop.
23261-oowikapun-or-how-the-gospel-reache:
Oowikapun tells how the gospel reached the Nelson River Indians, through the life of a young Indigenous hunter. His simple, quiet, monotonous life is broken in upon in a way he cannot undo. He can never be the same again after what reaches him.

A decided awakening has come. The circle of his vision has suddenly widened, and he has become aware that he is something more than he had imagined. The tale is a missionary story told from inside that change of mind. Readers get a period account of faith arriving in a northern hunting community, and of one young man's response.
a-lady-s-life-in-the-rocky-mountains: Isabella Bird's letters from her 1873 solo ride through the Colorado Rockies, then a wild frontier. This proper Englishwoman climbed peaks, survived blizzards, and befriended desperadoes, writing it all home with wit and grit. One of the great Victorian travel books, it proves that the boldest explorers were not always men.
a-rogue-s-life-by-wilkie-collins: A Rogue's Life by Wilkie Collins. The rogue's tale. This book preserves that Victorian novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
a-shepherd-s-life-impressions-of-the-sou: W. H. Hudson's Shepherd's Life preserves old Caleb Bawcombe and the vanishing world of the Wiltshire downs — a shepherd's year in loving detail. His record of rural England is now an elegy and a classic. Nature writing at its most humane.
a-tale-of-three-lions: H. Rider Haggard's 1887 Tale of Three Lions: African hunting adventure at its most thrilling. The great white hunter in action. Vintage Haggard, haggard's lions are Africa's kings, the hunt at its most thrilling, vintage Haggard adventure.
a-treatise-on-the-six-nation-indians: J. B. Mackenzie's study tells of the Six Nations, the great Iroquois league of Mohawks, Oneidas, Onondagas, Cayugas, Senecas, and Tuscaroras. He writes of their customs, their councils, and how this strong union of tribes held together long before white settlers came. A useful early record of one of North America's great native alliances.
a-waif-of-the-plains: A Bret Harte story about a waif of the plains: an orphan's adventures in the West. Tender and adventurous in his best manner. A fine example of his shorter fiction. Harte's orphans always find their home in the end.
actions-and-reactions: Actions and Reactions, Rudyard Kipling's story collection. The paired tales. This book preserves that collection. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
air-service-boys-in-the-big-battle-or-si: Charles Amory Beach sends his young American aviators into the great battles of the Western Front in this World War I adventure. Daring flights, dogfights with German aces, and a mission to silence the enemy's big guns keep the heroes aloft and in peril. Written while the war still raged, it thrilled boys with the newest, most romantic branch of service.
andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-military-: John McElroy's 1879 Andersonville: the rebel prison's horrors. The Civil War's most powerful memoir, harrowing and true. A national classic. The prison's horrors, harrowingly told, a national classic, harrowing and true, harrowing, true, and unforgettable, the Civil War's most powerful memoir.
b09-luther-hymns:
Martin Luther wrote hymns as well as tracts, and the songs may have carried his cause furthest of all. The hymns here, Deutsche Geistliche Lieder, begin in 1524, when his first songbooks appeared. Among them stands A Mighty Fortress Is Our God, still sung around the world.

German texts stand with English versions, and the tunes are printed with the words. Leonard Woolsey Bacon edited the set in 1884 for singers and scholars alike. Luther held that music drives out sorrow and teaches faith to the young. These pages show the Reformation as people actually sang it, in church, school, and home.
bandelier-hemenway-contributions:
Bandelier wrote his Contributions for the Hemenway Expedition, and they appeared in 1890. The Swiss-American scholar rebuilt the Southwest's written past from the archives. Pueblo and Spanish colonial history had never been traced with such care.

Dusty records in Mexico yield towns, missions, and peoples long lost. Bandelier sorts true reports from myth and mere boast by hard proof. His pages trace how Spain entered the region and what it found. Later digs and studies across the Southwest rest on this base. The book remains bedrock for the region's early history in print. Its notes still guide researchers through the archives today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-leri: This entry treats Lérins, the island abbey off Cannes. Honoratus founded it in the fifth century. Jean Besse sings its island praise. Saints have prayed there for sixteen hundred years. Vincent's Commonitory was written on its sunny shore. Two saints named Honoratus made it holy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain: This piece covers St. Albans, the English abbey of the first martyr. Alban's blood hallowed the Hertfordshire hill. Gilbert Huddleston gives its long history. A premier abbey of England. Matthew Paris chronicled England's kings within its walls. Its shrine drew pilgrims from every shire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abecedarians: This 1913 reference article on the Abecedarians — the sect that scorned all book learning. John Joseph A'Becket tells their strange story. They burned books and shunned schools. Fanaticism's war on the alphabet. Luther himself argued against their book-burning zeal. Their hatred of letters died with the sect itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-janss: This 1913 reference article on Abraham Janssens — the Flemish painter of grand baroque scenes. George Williamson surveys his canvases. Antwerp's churches still show his work. A solid master of the Counter-Reformation. His Day and Night hang in the Vienna gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acclamation-i: A 1913 entry on acclamation in papal elections — choosing a pope by sudden unanimous shout. William Fanning notes its rare use. The Spirit moves the cardinals as one. Rome's most dramatic elections. Gregory VII was hailed by the Roman crowd. Such moments were rare and momentous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-roman: This 1913 reference article on the acts of the Roman Congregations — decrees of the Vatican's high courts. Hector Papi explains their force and form. Cardinals judged the Church's causes. Rome's tribunals, and their written word. Their Latin filled the canonists' manuals. Every diocese felt their rulings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocates-of-: This 1913 reference piece on the advocates of the Roman Congregations — the canon lawyers who plead at Rome. William Fanning describes their college. They argue causes before the cardinals. The bar of the Vatican's courts. Learned pleaders in red-tape robes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aeons: This 1913 reference piece on the aeons — the shadowy emanations of Gnostic myth. John Bertram Peterson untangles their ranks. Valentinians counted thirty in all. Heresy built heavens of fancy. A guide through Gnostic mazes. Irenaeus mocked their fanciful family tree. Their names still puzzle the curious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agents-of-rom: A 1913 entry on the agents of the Roman Congregations — the business men who transacted causes at Rome. William Fanning explains their office. Bishops hired them to plead and pay. The Vatican's antechambers knew them well. Church business, professionally done. Their fees filled the manuals of style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexian-nuns: A 1913 entry on the Alexian Nuns — the sisters who nurse the sick. The entry traces their charitable rule. Their hospitals serve the suffering. The order's mercy knows no bounds. Handmaids of the sick poor. Their wards comfort the dying. Their veil is black, their work white.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexians: This 1913 reference article on the Alexians — the Cellite brothers of the sickbed. John Joseph A'Becket gives their history. They nursed plague victims fearlessly. Their houses spread through Germany. Charity's humble religious family. Their rule is St. Augustine's own. Their motherhouse stands in Aachen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-algonquins: A 1913 entry on the Algonquins — the great Indian family of the northeast woods. Thomas Campbell tells their mission story. The black robes lived and died among them. Their language family spans a continent. A noble race, sorely tried. Their missions dot the Great Lakes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-horns: A 1913 entry on altar horns — the raised corners of the old altars. Augustin Schulte traces them to Scripture. The Jewish altar bore such horns. Refugees clung to them for mercy. An ancient form, long kept. Their gilding caught the candlelight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-lantern: This 1913 reference article on altar lanterns — the lights of procession. Augustin Schulte describes their carrying. Their flames guard the Host's progress. Corpus Christi glows with their train. The Eucharist's moving guard. Their glass shields the flame from wind. Their poles bear the guilds' badges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-linens: This 1913 reference piece on altar linens — corporals, purificators, and palls. Augustin Schulte details each one's care. Their washing is a reverent rite. In that interview, Britain's Secret Intelligence Service is tied to the 1953 kidnapping of Tehran's chief of police. A kidnapping of the capital's police chief was no side detail in a coup; it removed a man who could have resisted. The posting links film research with the declassified record, each strengthening the other.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Doc:
Relations between Iran and the United States from 1978 to 2015 fill this National Security Archive collection. Those years run from the last period of the Shah's rule, through the revolution and hostage crisis, to the nuclear deal era. A documentary set spanning that whole arc is rare.

Most accounts treat those decades as separate stories: revolution, war, sanctions, talks. A single collection lets readers trace the same two governments across all of them. The value is continuity. Claims made in one decade can be checked against the paper of the next, which is exactly what a relations archive should allow.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Preoccupations with West Germany's Nuclear Weapons Potential: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
When Bill Clinton took office in January 1993, Boris Yeltsin's Russia was the new partner the United States had to learn to work with. The National Security Archive's electronic briefing book covers the first six months of that relationship. It is built on declassified records of the summits the two presidents held at Vancouver and in Tokyo that year.

The records show joint diplomatic work and a strikingly personal element: Clinton backed Yeltsin directly in his fight with the Russian parliament. That support helped set the tone for years of American policy toward Moscow. For readers, the papers capture a brief season when Washington treated Russia's shaky new democracy as a project worth personal risk from an American president.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_chile-cold-war-he:
Henry Kissinger shaped American foreign policy in the 1970s, and few figures of that era draw stronger praise or sharper blame. Under the heading Power by Any Means Necessary, the National Security Archive assembled a declassified dossier on his record. It is drawn from the secret files of the governments he dealt with, and of the one he served.

A dossier built from declassified papers lets readers test the legend against the memos. Kissinger, often shortened to HAK in the files of the time, left an unusually full paper trail across wars, coups, and secret diplomacy. The collection's value is that it argues with documents rather than opinion, giving critics and defenders alike the same evidence to work from.
graded-lessons-in-english-an-elementary-: Reed and Kellogg's graded lessons taught generations of American schoolchildren to diagram sentences and master English grammar. One hundred practical lessons built solid foundations, sentence by sentence. The classic American grammar that shaped how the nation learned to write well.
happy-hawkins: Happy Hawkins is a cheerful and breezy western novel. Its easygoing hero drifts through ranch life with a ready grin. Trouble finds him often, but good humor always saves the day. A lighthearted tale of the old West.
human-nature-and-other-sermons: Bishop Butler’s famed sermons on human nature and conscience. They hold the deepest moral thought of the 1700s. His calm wisdom has guided readers for centuries. Profound and measured throughout, profound and measured, calm and wise.
hunted-down-the-detective-stories-of-cha: Dickens's ventures into crime fiction, led by the title story of a detective hunting a murderer through an insurance fraud. Though better known for novels, Dickens created some of the earliest detective stories in English, full of fog, pursuit, and moral dread. This collection gathers his scattered tales of crime and detection in one volume.
indian-heroes-and-great-chieftains: Eastman's Indian Heroes (1918) profiles great chiefs. Courage honored. The Tower library holds the full text. It heroed Indians. Chiefs led. Battles raged. Honor stood. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
intentions: Oscar Wilde's 1891 collection of critical essays, including "The Decay of Lying" and "The Critic as Artist." In dialogue form and with outrageous wit, Wilde argues that art should be useless, beautiful, and superior to life itself. These essays are the intellectual engine of the aesthetic movement, and some of the funniest criticism ever written.
jimmie-higgins:
Jimmie Higgins is a novel by Upton Sinclair, the American writer known for exposing social wrongs. Its contents page alone maps Jimmie's whole path in twenty chapter titles. He meets a candidate, hears a speech, and debates the issue. Then he strikes it rich, helps the Kaiser, and goes to jail.

Later chapters send Jimmie back to nature, face to face with an owner, and into open war. He meets a patriot, dodges trouble, and takes the road. The titles then turn sharp: Jimmie turns Bolshevik, meets a tempter, and wrestles with him. At last he takes the plunge and puts on khaki. Sinclair builds a working man's political education into a story.
journals-of-australian-explorations:
Journals of Australian Explorations gathers the expedition journals of Augustus Charles Gregory and his brother Francis Thomas Gregory. Both men were fellows of the Royal Geographical Society and gold medalists of it. The Brisbane government printer issued the volume in 1884. Its preface explains that readers kept asking for journals long out of print.

Earlier, the journals had appeared only in fragments. This volume collects them whole, for reference and for the permanent record. It leaves the brothers' first impressions unchanged, even where later knowledge corrected them. The first journal covers the 1846 expedition east and north of Swan River. A settlers' expedition under A. C. Gregory in 1848 follows. Together they trace early attempts to open Australia's unknown interior.
judith-of-the-plains:
Judith of the Plains is a novel by Marie Manning, published by Harper and Brothers in 1903. Twenty chapters carry the story, opening simply with Town. Judith works as postmistress, as one chapter title announces. Leander and his lady, the Rodneys at home, and Mrs. Yellett and her 'government' fill the early cast.

The plot moves onto the horse-thief trail and into a cabin in the valley. A round-up, a wolf hunt, and the land of the red silence follow. Mary spends her first day in camp, and Judith adjusts the situation. Cloudburst, hanging threats, and a final ball close the contents. Manning writes a Western of ranch life with a capable heroine at its center.
keith-of-the-border-a-tale-of-the-plains:
Keith of the Border: A Tale of the Plains is a Western novel by Randall Parrish. Thirty-six chapters carry it from The Plainsman to The End. Early chapters stage a sudden arrest and a desperate escape. A ride through sand and desert leads to a wilderness cabin and the girl there.

Keith crosses the ford of the Arkansas and reaches the marshal of Sheridan. Christie Maclaire enters as one who believes in him, and a message from the dead complicates his case. An Indian raid, a duel in the desert, and a single shot raise the stakes. The final chapters bring forgiveness and a last interview. Parrish writes fast frontier adventure around a wronged plainsman clearing his name.
life-of-charles-dickens:
Frank T. Marzials wrote this Dickens life for the Great Writers series. Walter Scott published it in London in 1887. Marzials acknowledges a heavy debt to Forster's life of Dickens. He also used the letters edited by Dickens's family.

Charles Dickens was born on February 7, 1812. Happy Chatham days gave way to family troubles and London hardship. His father entered the Marshalsea, and Charles worked in a blacking business. Marzials compares the boy's isolation with David Copperfield's story. Kitton's Dickensiana lightened Marzials's labor considerably, he acknowledges. Young Charles felt isolation keenly during the blacking warehouse months.
lives-of-the-three-mrs-judsons:
Arabella M. Willson wrote these lives of three missionary wives. Ann, Sarah, and Emily Judson each married the same missionary. All three served as missionaries to Burmah in turn. Lee and Shepard published the book in Boston.

Congress copyright records date its entry to 1855. Portraits of Ann and Emily Judson illustrate the volume. A verse epigraph praises their self-denying band of workers. They counted life cheap to fulfil their ministry, it says. Miller, Orton and Mulligan first entered the copyright in 1855. Charles Dillingham later sold the New York edition.
love-among-the-chickens:
Love Among the Chickens is an early comic novel by P. G. Wodehouse. In his dedication, Wodehouse thanks his friend W. Townend for giving him the stuff. Sixteen years before, he says, they were sprightly lads at school together. The stuff Townend gave him became a chicken farm by the sea.

A young writer joins his friend's hopeless chicken venture on the coast. Hens, eggs, and farm chaos fill the days there. Amid the squawking, the young man falls in love. Wodehouse keeps the tone light, bright, and full of jokes. The book shows his high spirits long before his fame peaked. It is vintage early Wodehouse, warm and very funny.
men-like-gods-dover-thrift-editions:
H. G. Wells published this utopian novel in 1923. Its hero, Mr. Barnstaple, is a tired journalist who takes a holiday drive in 1921. He and several other motorists are suddenly swept three thousand years into the future. This Dover edition reprints the original Macmillan text.

The travelers land in a world remade along Barnstaple's own ideals. Crime, poverty, war, disease, and bigotry have all vanished there. Wells uses the visit to test his hopes for science and social planning. The novel asks whether ordinary modern people could bear such a perfected world, or would spoil it.
missionary-work-among-the-ojebway-indian:
The Reverend Edward F. Wilson tells here how he came to work among the Ojibway of Canada. His contents trace the journey: first experiences, arrival at Sarnia, and work at Kettle Point. He records Indian names given to the missionaries and a Christmas spent on the reserve. The bishop's visit and a first trip to Garden River follow.

Later chapters describe baptisms of pagan Indians and the Red River expedition. Wilson meets Chief Little Pine and winters in Algoma. His account preserves detail about Ojibway life, language, and customs in his era. Mission memoirs like his remain sources, read critically, for nineteenth-century Indigenous history around the Great Lakes.
modern-italian-poets-essays-and-versions:
William Dean Howells wrote these essays on Italy's modern poets, adding his own English versions of their verse. The contents begin with the Arcadian shepherds of the eighteenth century. Giuseppe Parini, Vittorio Alfieri, and Vincenzo Monti follow. Ugo Foscolo and Alessandro Manzoni anchor the Romantic generation.

Howells gives Giacomo Leopardi a place among the later names. Giuseppe Giusti, Giovanni Prati, and Aleardo Aleardi continue the line to his own century. Silvio Pellico, famous for his prison memoir, appears as a poet here. Howells, America's leading novelist-critic of his day, introduced English readers to Italian poetry he had loved since his consulate at Venice.
more-toasts-jokes-stories-and-quotations:
Marion Dix Mosher, a Rochester public librarian, compiled this handbook in 1922. The H. W. Wilson Company published it at New York. At 552 pages it promises jokes, stories, and quotations for speakers. The contents open with an essay on the importance of humor.

That essay, reprinted from the Nineteenth Century, calls humor a divine gift. It deals, the essay says, with a mystery pleasantly woven into daily life. Toasts fill the body of the book, with an index for finding them fast. Banquet speakers and toastmasters of the 1920s kept such compilations at hand, and librarians like Mosher built them for reference shelves.
mother-carey-s-chickens:
Kate Douglas Wiggin opens this family story with the petrels called Mother Carey's chickens. The birds flit from wave to wave like swallows over the sea. Mother Carey herself heads the first chapter, and her chickens the second. A chapter called The Common Denominator introduces the family's shared life.

Then comes The Broken Circle, and the Careys' flitting, or move, to Beulah. Cousin Ann, a service on the threshold, and a housewarming mark the new home. Nancy's idea and Nancy's coming out carry the eldest girl forward. Wiggin, author of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, writes of a widowed mother holding her brood together with cheer.
my-literary-passions:
William Dean Howells maps his reading life in this 1895 book. The contents begin with the bookcase at home. Goldsmith, Cervantes, and Irving mark his early loves. First fiction and drama follow, then Scott and Pope.

Uncle Tom's Cabin, Ossian, and Shakespeare each get a chapter. Dickens, Thackeray, Dante, and Tolstoy mark later stages. He ends with new names like Zola, Hardy, and Galdos. Howells tells how each book formed his taste and craft. The memoir is a reader's autobiography, warm and exact, showing how one boy's shelf became an American man of letters.
nasa-tm-19650015349-1964-publications:
Compiled by the Materials Division at Marshall and dated January 30, 1965, this volume lists NASA publications from 1964. The entries are technical notes from across the agency's programs. Subjects run from materials and propulsion to spacecraft and engineering development work of many kinds.

A yearly list like this one served as a finding aid. Researchers could scan one volume to see what the agency had released. They could then order the notes that mattered to their own work. As a record, it also freezes one busy year in place. The range of titles shows how wide NASA's technical work had become by 1964.
nasa-tm-19660020445-an-approximate-solut:
Peter Ralph Kurzhals submitted this work in May 1966 as a doctoral thesis at Virginia Polytechnic Institute. His subject is the motion of a rotating spacecraft of any shape. Real spacecraft tumble or spin in complex ways, pushed by small uneven forces. Kurzhals offers an approximate analytic solution for that motion, with disturbance effects that can vary over time.

Exact solutions exist only for simple, tidy shapes. Flight vehicles are neither simple nor tidy. An approximate solution that handles arbitrary shapes fills a real gap. Disturbance functions stand for the small torques that slowly change a spin in flight. Thesis work of this depth, done inside the space program, fed directly into attitude control practice.
nasa-tm-19680013932-biosatellite-2-opera:
John W. Dyer of NASA's Ames Research Center presented this account of Biosatellite II operations in February 1968. The spacecraft carried living specimens into orbit so scientists could study how space flight affects life. Dyer explains how the mission was planned, flown, and recovered using services that already existed.

The craft weighed about 950 pounds and rode a two-stage Delta launch vehicle. About half its weight sat in the reentry vehicle that returned the specimens to Earth. Batteries supplied power, since the smooth craft carried no solar panels. Gas jets and gyroscopes held rotation very slow, keeping forces on the specimens small during the flight.
nasa-tm-19680016151-morphological-studie:
Webb Haymaker of NASA's Ames Research Center reviews studies of laminar lesions in the brain in this essay, prepared in 1967. The cerebral cortex has six thin layers, or laminae. Researchers asked whether one layer could be destroyed while the others stayed intact.

If one layer alone could be removed, its role in cortical electrical activity could be tested. An early study used proton radiation on cats to damage a narrow zone of cortex. That work, reported ten years earlier, showed selective damage was feasible. Haymaker surveys the morphology, or physical form, of such lesions. Dose and tissue volume factors shape how the damage develops in the cortex.
nasa-tm-19700009336-low-frequency-cosmic:
Four Goddard Space Flight Center researchers, J. K. Alexander, L. W. Brown, T. A. Clark, and R. G. Stone, wrote this preprint on low frequency cosmic noise. Cosmic noise is the steady radio hiss arriving from our own galaxy. Their question is what that hiss reveals about the local system of stars and gas near Earth.

Working from galaxy-wide radio measurements, the team estimates how thermal electrons are spread through nearby space. They also estimate the glow from fast electrons spiraling in magnetic fields, plus the flow of low energy cosmic ray electrons. Their radio figures run far above direct measurements, by about a hundredfold. They suggest strong solar effects or an uneven cosmic ray spread could explain the gap.
nasa-tm-19710023966-the-degeneration-of-:
H. Volland and H. G. Mayr of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in August 1971, numbered X-621-71-331. It concerns Hough functions, the mathematical shapes that describe atmospheric tides in the lower atmosphere. The authors ask what happens to those shapes high in the thermosphere, where dissipation takes hold.

Heat conduction, viscosity, and drag between neutral air and ions all modify the Hough functions as height increases. The paper shows they ultimately degenerate into spherical harmonics above about two hundred kilometers. That degeneration changes the latitude structure of the tidal modes and how waves travel upward. In particular, the twice-daily tidal mode becomes nearly trapped above about one hundred sixty kilometers, explaining its apparent absence in upper thermosphere dynamics.
nasa-tm-19720007680-review-of-magnetic-f:
Norman F. Ness of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this review in November 1971, numbered X-690-71-465, on magnetic field observations in the magnetosphere. By then satellites were routinely mapping Earth's magnetic bubble and its boundaries. Ness gathered the recent observations into one account of what they showed.

The review describes improved pictures of the magnetosphere, magnetosheath, plasma sheet, and bow shock, and how storms distort them. Observations of the polar cusp region support the idea that particles reach the plasma sheet through the polar neutral points. Distortions there suggest currents flowing along field lines far from Earth. The plasma sheet's field reversal region proved more complex than simple single neutral line models. No clear solar cycle change in magnetosphere structure was detected.
navy-boys-behind-the-big-guns:
Halsey Davidson wrote Navy Boys Behind the Big Guns as a sea adventure for boys. Its subtitle is Sinking the German U-Boats, which places it in the First World War. George Sully and Company published it in New York, with pictures. Davidson had written other Navy Boys books before this one.

A front picture shows gunners stripped for action, alert as panthers, by their guns. The series list names Navy Boys After the Submarines and Navy Boys Chasing a Sea Raider. Sea fights, convoys, and prizes fill those titles. Young readers of the war years got their navy's fight told as fast, brave action close to the guns.
new-tabernacle-sermons:
T. De Witt Talmage preached the sermons in New Tabernacle Sermons at the Brooklyn Tabernacle. George Munro published volume one in New York in 1886. Talmage had already issued Crumbs Swept Up and The Abominations of Modern Society. A portrait of the preacher fronts the book.

Sermon titles range from Brawn and Muscle to The Pleiades and Orion. The Queen's Visit, Vicarious Suffering, and The Lord's Razor follow. Windows Toward Jerusalem, The Great Assize, and The Road to the City keep the biblical frame. One late sermon takes up capital and labor. Talmage spoke to city crowds on faith, duty, and the day they lived in.
options:
O. Henry gathered sixteen short stories in Options, one of his late collections of tales built on surprise endings and city-and-country contrasts. The table of contents names pieces such as The Third Ingredient, The Hiding of Black Bill, Supply and Demand, Buried Treasure, The Higher Pragmatism, Best-Seller, and Rus in Urbe.

The opening story, The Rose of Dixie, starts in Toombs City, Georgia, where a stock company has raised a hundred thousand dollars to found a magazine. A committee calls on Colonel Aquila Telfair, a man of learning, family, and Southern tradition, to beg him to edit it. O. Henry sets the scene in the colonel's inherited library of ten thousand volumes, and the comedy of old South meeting new publishing begins.
osage-traditions:
James Owen Dorsey was a missionary-linguist for the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology. He recorded Osage Traditions in Indian Territory in January 1883. A secret society of seven degrees guarded the people's traditions, he learned. His short stay allowed only fragments. Initiated Osage men gave him parts of two traditions.

Red Corn, of the Tsiu washtake gens, dictated the first tradition. He had it from Sadekihe. Red Corn's own story fills much of the introduction. A white man adopted him. He studied at a Jesuit college in Missouri. Later he practiced as an Indian doctor, known to whites as Bill Nix. The pamphlet preserves sacred tradition and the tale of its telling.
our-churches-and-chapels-their-parsons-p:
A. Hewitson, writing as Atticus in the Preston Chronicle, surveyed every place of worship in Preston. Churches, chapels, parsons, priests, and congregations all came under his eye. He reprinted the sketches as a book in 1869. His preface warns readers that a lively spirit runs through the descriptions, which may offend the phlegmatic, the sad-faced, and the puritanical.

Hewitson promises the solemn their facts, the facetious their humour, and the analytical their criticism. The work embodies a fuller history of each Preston place of worship than any yet published, he claims. The town's Anglican, Catholic, and Dissenting clergy helped generously. Genial humour, he insists, only makes the dry enumeration palatable.
out-with-gun-and-camera-or-the-boy-hunte:
Edward Stratemeyer, writing as Captain Ralph Bonehill, sent his boy hunters into the mountains in Out with Gun and Camera, the fourth volume of the Boy Hunters Series. Its thirty chapters promise adventures with rod, rifle, shotgun, and camera. A lesson in photography comes early. Then the circus, the river rapids, and a cabin in the woods. A fight with two wildcats waits later, and a bear and a lion.

In his preface, addressed my dear lads, Stratemeyer says the series aims to acquaint boys with field, forest, river, and lake in winter and summer. The stories are complete in themselves. The hunting is half sporting manual. Game is photographed as well as shot. The Spink crowd returns as the standing enemy.
over-there-with-the-australians:
Captain R. Hugh Knyvett, an ANZAC scout and intelligence officer of the Fifteenth Australian Infantry, published Over There with the Australians with Scribner's in April 1918. He would not survive the year. The book opens not with his prose but with a poem, Bill-Jim's Christmas — Bill-Jim being Australia's name for her soldier.

Bill-Jim sits mucked up with Flanders mud. Pests he will not name to polite ears eat at him. Still he insists he is glad to be there. A man must fight for freedom and his blood. He must not growl while doing it. Then the homesickness breaks through: God, give me Christmas Day in Sydney town, and the flowers in Martin Place. Knyvett's memoir carries that double note — endurance and longing — through the Australian war.
peter-pan-in-kensington-gardens:
Barrie's Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens tells of Peter before Neverland. If you ask your grandmother about Peter, the narrator says, she knew him, but he had no goat in her day. Peter is ever so old, yet always one week of age, and he has never had a birthday.

At seven days old he escaped by the window and flew back to the Kensington Gardens, remembering that babies were birds before they were human. The short contents promise the thrush's nest, the little house, and lock-out time. It is a gentler, stranger Peter Pan book, full of fairies and the lore of birds.
plays-and-puritans:
Charles Kingsley's Plays and Puritans comes from his book of historical essays, in the Macmillan edition of 1890. Kingsley was a clergyman, novelist, and historian. The essay asks why the English stage and the arts around it seemed weak in his own day.

Kingsley argues that most Britons of his time cared little for art, however much the word was praised. He traces that cool temper back to the old Puritans, softened and widened over time. The middle classes, he says, liked art only when it meant nothing and stayed in its place.
podcast-joerogan-DBO5VRwGYns:
Satirist Seth Dillon joins Joe Rogan to react to the FBI raid on Donald Trump's home. Dillon runs the Babylon Bee, a joke news site. Trump had shared Bee posts many times, to Dillon's delight.

Dillon argues the raid poured fuel on Trump's support and fundraising. Rogan asks what agents found and what charges might follow. They weigh legal risk against political gain in plain terms. The episode mixes comedy-shop talk with a live read on a raid that reshaped a campaign before either man knew the full facts. It stays lively throughout.
podcast-joerogan-Ru7BIqXQZns:
Dr. Mary Talley Bowden joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2335. Bowden is a Texas doctor who clashed with hospitals and boards over her COVID treatment views, and her fight made her a hero to skeptics of the official line. Rogan hosts her to state that case.

She tells Rogan what she prescribed, what it cost her, and why she would not back down. Rogan asks about the patients she says recovered and the data fights behind the headlines. The episode preserves a dissenting doctor's full account, the kind of testimony his audience seeks out and his critics dispute.
podcast-joerogan-c6JdeL90ans:
Jeremie and Edouard Harris return to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2156, an earlier visit from the Gladstone AI brothers. The twins had already begun warning officials about advanced AI risks. This talk updates their case as the machines' march speeds up.

The brothers explain the gap between what labs can build and what governments understand. They share scenarios where control slips away step by reasonable step. Rogan asks how close the danger is and who is minding the store. Tech-wary and thoughtful listeners get a warning that has only grown louder since.
podcast-joerogan-mNPM0yUiyNs:
Michio Kaku returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1828. Kaku, the string-theory physicist and tireless explainer, uses his return to look ahead: the future, the cosmos, and the next big leaps for science and for our species. He is in fine form, as Rogan fans expect.

He sketches the coming century as he sees it, from fusion and space travel to contact with other minds. Rogan asks which leaps he will live to see. The episode is a bold, cheerful forecast from a man who has spent his life telling the public that the impossible is usually just early.
poems-and-songs-of-robert-burns: The essential Burns: "Auld Lang Syne," "My Heart's in the Highlands," "Tam o' Shanter," and dozens more songs and poems in Scots and English. Ploughman-poet of Ayrshire, Burns wrote of love, drink, democracy, and mice with unmatched warmth. This collection gathers the work that made him Scotland's national bard.
red-pepper-burns: Grace Richmond's Red Pepper Burns: the peppery doctor's romance. Warm and humorous in the popular style. A beloved novel of its day. Richmond's red pepper is romance with a tang, the doctor's love story, warm and humorous.
rose-in-bloom-a-sequel-to-eight-cousins: Louisa May Alcott's 1876 Rose in Bloom: Rose grown up, and her cousins' courtship. The sequel to Eight Cousins, warm and wise. A beloved conclusion. Rose blooms into womanhood, alcott's farewell to her cousins, Alcott's farewell.
sintram-and-his-companions: Young Sintram fights the dark powers that dog his house. Fouqué’s 1814 fable of sin and grace is strange and lovely. A haunting German romance. A tale to read by winter firelight, strange and lovely.
sixes-and-sevens: O. Henry's 1911 Sixes and Sevens: his last stories, published after his death. The twist master's farewell, still sparkling. New York's chronicler bows out. O. Henry's farewell is still full of tricks, the last twists, the twist master's farewell collection.
somerville-recollections:
Mary Somerville published her Personal Recollections in 1873, a year after her death, through her daughter's care. Somerville had been called the queen of science for her books on astronomy and physics. She wrote science clearly when few women could publish at all.

She recalls a Scottish girlhood with almost no schooling, then a late, self-driven turn to math. London drawing rooms brought her Herschel, Laplace's circle, and the whole Victorian scientific world. Her memory for people and places stayed keen into her nineties. The recollections show how one determined woman joined the highest ranks of science.
speaking-of-operations: Irvin Cobb's humorous 1915 book about his own operation: hospitals, surgeons, and the patient's point of view, told with his Southern wit. Funny and human, it made surgery entertaining. A classic of American humor. Cobb's Southern humor turns even ether into entertainment.
susy-a-story-of-the-plains: Bret Harte's Susy: a story of the plains, a girl's adventures in the West. Charming and colorful in his best manner. A fine Western tale. Harte's Susy is a true daughter of the West, brave and charming.
sybil-or-the-two-nations: Sybil, or The Two Nations, Benjamin Disraeli's political novel. The rich and poor. This book preserves that classic. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
tanakh-jps-1917-lamentations: Five funeral songs for a ruined city. Jerusalem has fallen to Babylon, and the poet sits in the ashes asking how this happened — yet clinging to hope: “great is thy faithfulness.” This 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation gives the Bible's book of grief in moving English.
the-acharnians: Aristophanes's 425 BC Acharnians: the first surviving comedy. Dicaeopolis makes his private peace. The birth of comedy, wild and brilliant. Comedy's birth, wild and brilliant, the first laugh, the birth of comedy, Dicaeopolis makes peace, the first surviving comedy.
the-adventure-of-the-bruce-partington-pl: Holmes on the Bruce-Partington plans: stolen submarine plans and a body on the Underground tracks. Mycroft calls, and the fate of England hangs on the case. Espionage and deduction at their finest. Colonel Valentine Walter's treason nearly sank England.
the-albert-n-yanza-great-basin-of-the-ni: Baker's The Albert N'Yanza chronicles the great search for the Nile's source. The tireless explorer crossed Africa to find the great lake. Hardship and discovery fill the stirring narrative throughout. A true landmark in the history of exploration.
the-bandolero-or-a-marriage-among-the-mo: The Bandolero, or A Marriage among the Mountains, by Mayne Reid. The brigand's wedding. This book preserves that novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
the-belgian-twins: The Belgian Twins is a children's story set in wartime Belgium. A brave brother and sister flee the invading armies with courage and hope. Young readers meet great history through young and lively eyes. A gentle tale of a very hard time, told with warmth.
the-burial-of-the-guns: Nelson's Burial of the Guns (1894) mourns Confederate artillery. The South remembers. The Tower library holds the full text. It buried guns. Cannons silenced. Veterans wept. the-collegians: The Collegians, Gerald Griffin's Irish novel. The college tale. This book preserves that story. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Those who study the era will use it in their work.

Delegates of the eighteenth General Assembly heard John F. Kennedy on September 20, 1963, in what became the last major foreign address of his presidency. The Limited Test Ban Treaty had been signed that summer by the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union. Kennedy came to New York to build on that step.

The address hails the test ban and urges further curbs on nuclear arms. It proposes joint work in space, even a shared voyage to the Moon. It also speaks to new nations and the poor. Two months later Kennedy was killed, which lends the speech its lasting glow.
un-un-res-ahmadinejad-s-2005-address-to-:

Ahmadinejad defended Iran's right to develop nuclear energy for peaceful use. He accused the big powers of hoarding nuclear know-how while denying it to others. He also called for reform of the Security Council. The address set the tone for years of standoff between Iran and the West.
un-un-res-constitution-of-the-food-and-a:
Feeding a hungry world was written into the founding charter of the Food and Agriculture Organization, adopted in 1945. The FAO was the first specialized agency of the new United Nations. Its constitution set the agency's aims, members, and rules of work at the close of the Second World War.

The text pledges states to raise nutrition, improve farm output, and better the lives of rural people. It creates the conference, council, and director-general who run the agency. Every FAO program since rests on this charter, which makes it a root document of world food policy.
un-un-res-report-of-the-secretary-genera:
Paying for the first United Nations Emergency Force is the subject of this 1956 report of the Secretary-General, document A/3383. The force had been created in haste during the Suez Crisis, and no budget line existed for it. How to fund it fairly among member states was a hard, new question.

The report sets out the force's expected costs and options for sharing them. It deals with pay, supply, transport, and claims for harm or loss. The funding model worked out here shaped how later peacekeeping forces were paid for, a fight that still flares at the UN.
unconscious-comedians: One of Balzac's shorter Parisian studies: a young man from the provinces learns how the capital's artists, journalists, and lawyers really live. where-the-blue-begins: Christopher Morley's 1922 fantasy about Gissing, a dog who runs a shop and yearns for something more, setting out on a quest for the place "where the blue begins." Charming, philosophical, and gently funny, it is a fable for grown-ups who still wonder.
xenophon-agesilaus-dakyns:
Xenophon campaigned under Sparta's King Agesilaus II and admired him deeply. His short Agesilaus praises the king as a model ruler, and H. G. Dakyns translated it into English. It ranks among the earliest royal biographies ever written.

Xenophon praises Agesilaus for bravery, plain habits, loyalty, and decency toward enemies. Campaigns in Asia and Greece show the king sharing hardship with his soldiers. The praise is one-sided, since Xenophon wrote as a devoted follower. Still, the portrait set a pattern later biographers copied for centuries. Dakyns's clear English carries the Greek across without fuss.
xenophon-anabasis-dakyns:
Xenophon's Anabasis recounts the march of the Ten Thousand through Persia around 370 BCE. H. G. Dakyns translated the famous narrative into English. Xenophon marched with the army and became one of its leaders.

Ten thousand Greek mercenaries found themselves stranded deep inside the Persian Empire. Their employer dead, they elected new generals and marched for home. Mountains, snow, and hostile tribes blocked the road to the sea. The shout of 'The sea, the sea' became literature's great homecoming moment. Xenophon's account doubles as a firsthand window onto the ancient Near East. Dakyns keeps the march at a soldier's pace throughout.
xenophon-apology-dakyns:
Xenophon wrote his Apology to record how Socrates defended himself at trial in Athens. H. G. Dakyns translated the short work into English. Athens had charged Socrates with corrupting the young and impiety.

Socrates refuses to beg the court for mercy or pity. He argues that death now spares him the decay of extreme old age. His calm before the hemlock impressed followers as proof of his teaching. Xenophon's version is shorter and plainer than Plato's famous Apology. Together they give two ancient voices on philosophy's most famous trial. Dakyns keeps the soldierly plainness of Xenophon's style.
xenophon-cavalry-general-dakyns:
Xenophon wrote The Cavalry General for the officer taking command of Athens' horsemen. H. G. Dakyns translated the brisk manual into English. Xenophon had led cavalry in real campaigns across Greece and Asia.

He covers choosing officers, training riders, and keeping horses fit and calm. Chapters treat scouting, orderly retreats, and keeping up the men's spirits. Religious duties and festival processions also belong to the commander's job. The advice stays practical throughout, with nothing merely theoretical. Dakyns's translation keeps the no-nonsense tone of a soldier instructing soldiers. Modern officers still recognize the leadership problems Xenophon names.
xenophon-cyropaedia-dakyns:
Xenophon's Cyropaedia imagines the education and rise of Cyrus the Great of Persia. H. G. Dakyns translated the long work into English. Part adventure tale and part handbook for rulers, it shaped political writing for centuries.

The young Cyrus learns justice, endurance, and command among Persian boys. As king he wins loyalty through fairness and shared hardship rather than fear. Xenophon uses Persia to ask how good rulers are made. Ancient kings studied the book, and Machiavelli read it closely later. It is less history than a mirror for princes. Dakyns's old-fashioned English suits its heroic glow.
xenophon-economist-dakyns:
Xenophon's Economist, or Oeconomicus, stages Socrates discussing how to run a household well. H. G. Dakyns translated the dialogue into English. In ancient Greek, economics meant managing a home and estate.

Socrates questions a young landowner about training servants and storing grain. Keeping accounts and ordering work receive careful, practical attention. The landowner's wife appears as a true partner in managing the estate. That partnership struck readers as unusual for ancient Greece. The dialogue ranks among the earliest works of economic writing anywhere. Dakyns's version reads like easy, good-humored conversation. The talk stays plain and warm from start to end.
xenophon-hellenica-dakyns:
Xenophon's Hellenica continues Greek history where Thucydides' famous account breaks off unfinished. H. G. Dakyns translated the seven books into English. The narrative covers nearly fifty years, down to 362 BCE.

Readers follow the end of the Peloponnesian War and Athens' surrender. Sparta rises to dominance, overreaches, and falls to Thebes at Leuctra. Xenophon writes as a soldier who knew many of the actors personally. His Spartan sympathies show, and some major events receive puzzling silence. Even so, no other continuous account survives for these years. Dakyns keeps the narrative moving briskly.
xenophon-hiero-dakyns:
Xenophon's Hiero stages a conversation between a Sicilian tyrant and the poet Simonides. H. G. Dakyns translated the dialogue into English. Hiero of Syracuse explains why absolute power has made him miserable.

The tyrant describes fear, flattery, and loneliness instead of expected pleasures. He cannot trust friends, enjoy travel, or sleep without guards. Simonides answers that a ruler serving his people might earn genuine love. He sketches reforms in policing, prizes, and public works. The dialogue stands among antiquity's frankest examinations of unchecked power. Dakyns's translation keeps the exchange sharp and readable. It is brief, blunt, and hard to put down.
xenophon-memorabilia-dakyns:
Xenophon's Memorabilia collects his recollections of Socrates in conversation over four books. H. G. Dakyns translated the work into English. Xenophon knew Socrates personally and wrote partly to defend his memory.

Athens had executed Socrates for corrupting the young and denying the gods. Xenophon answers by showing Socrates advising generals, craftsmen, and know-it-alls helpfully. His Socrates teaches clear thinking, self-control, and decent conduct in practical terms. This Socrates feels less lofty than Plato's, more like a man one might meet. Dakyns lets that down-to-earth voice come through plainly for modern readers.
xenophon-on-horsemanship-dakyns:
Xenophon wrote On Horsemanship from a cavalryman's lifetime of experience with horses. H. G. Dakyns translated the treatise into English. It is the first complete guide to riding and horse care that survives.

He explains how to judge a young horse before buying it. Fitting the bridle, training gently, and keeping a mount calm follow in order. Xenophon also treats stable management, grooming, and common injuries of war horses. His rule against anger in training still sounds modern and humane. Horse people quote his advice after more than two thousand years. Dakyns preserves the plain, expert voice throughout.
xenophon-on-revenues-dakyns:
Xenophon's On Revenues proposes how Athens could fill its treasury without new citizen taxes. H. G. Dakyns translated the short pamphlet into English. Athens faced money troubles after years of war and lost empire.

He urges working the silver mines at Laurium more intensively with public slaves. Better harbor facilities and honors would draw foreign traders to Piraeus. Public buildings and a merchant fleet could earn steady income for citizens. The plan reads like an ancient policy memo, hopeful and detailed. Some proposals were tried, others ignored by the assembly. Dakyns keeps the businesslike tone of the original pamphlet.
xenophon-polity-athenians-lacedaemonians:
Two short studies of Greek government stand side by side in Dakyns's translation. One sketch describes the constitution of Athens, the other that of Sparta. Tradition assigns both to Xenophon, though scholars debate the Athenian piece.

The Athenian sketch coolly explains why democracy served Athens' sea empire well. It sounds grudging, as if written by a critic admitting democracy works. The Spartan sketch admires the laws and training behind Sparta's soldiers. Lycurgus's discipline, common meals, and austere education receive warm praise. Together the pair gives priceless snapshots of rival constitutions. Few short texts teach Greek politics so efficiently.
xenophon-sportsman-dakyns:
Xenophon's Sportsman, or Cynegeticus, teaches hunting with hounds to young Greek gentlemen. H. G. Dakyns translated the treatise into English. For Xenophon, hunting trained men for war and for life itself.

He covers picking hounds, training them, and reading the tracks of game. Setting nets and standing firm before a charging boar receive detailed instruction. Reflections on courage, discipline, and honoring the hunt's gods interrupt the practical tips. Xenophon defends hunting against critics who called it a waste of time. Dakyns's translation carries the outdoorsman's enthusiasm of the original Greek throughout.
xenophon-symposium-dakyns:
Xenophon's Symposium places Socrates at a rich young man's dinner party in Athens. H. G. Dakyns translated the dialogue into English. Wine, dancing girls, and a comic strongman entertain the guests between speeches.

Socrates steers the talk toward love, beauty, and what makes a life worthwhile. Guests praise their own talents, and Socrates jokes about his looks and dancing. The tone stays lighter and livelier than Plato's famous Symposium. Xenophon's version feels like an actual evening among friends. Dakyns keeps the banter sparkling in translation. Readers get Socrates laughing, not only lecturing, for once.
